# Influenza Vaccination and Use of Lipid Lowering Therapies in Adults with Atherosclerotic Cardiovascular Disease: An Analysis of the Behavioral Risk Factor Surveillance System (BRFSS)

**Authors:** Samuel D. Slavin; Adam N. Berman; Prakriti Gaba; Rosangela A. Hoshi; Murray A. Mittleman

**Affiliations:** aBrigham and Women’s Hospital, Division of Cardiovascular Medicine, Boston, MA | bHarvard Medical School, Boston, MA | cBeth Israel Deaconess Medical Center, Boston, MA | dHarvard Chan School of Public Health, Division of Epidemiology, Boston, MA

## Abstract

Influenza vaccination and lipid lowering therapy (LLT) are evidence-based interventions with substantial benefit for individuals with established atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD). However, levels of influenza immunization and LLT use are low, possibly due to pervasive fear-based misinformation uniquely targeting vaccines and LLT. Whether being unvaccinated for influenza predicts lower utilization of LLT is unknown.

We tested the hypothesis that American adults with ASCVD who are unvaccinated for influenza have lower use of LLT even after accounting for traditional factors associated with underuse of preventive therapies.

We pooled 2017, 2019, and 2021 survey data from the Behavioral Risk Factor Surveillance System (BRFSS), and selected respondents aged 40 to 75 years with self-reported ASCVD. We used logistic regression models adjusted for potential confounders to examine the association between influenza vaccination and self-reported LLT use. We performed a sensitivity analysis with multiple imputation to account for missing data. All analyses accounted for complex survey weighting.

Of 66,923 participants with ASCVD, 55% reported influenza vaccination in the last year and 76% reported using LLT. Being unvaccinated for influenza was associated with lower odds of LLT use (OR 0.54; 95% CI 0.50, 0.58; p<0.001). In a multivariable regression model adjusting for demographics and co-morbidities, this association remained statistically significant (aOR 0.58, 95% CI 0.52, 0.64, p<0.001). After additional adjustment for preventive care engagement, health care access, and use patterns of other cardiovascular medications this association persisted (aOR 0.66; 95% CI 0.60, 0.74; p<0.001). There were no significant differences across sub-groups, including those with and without hyperlipidemia.

Unvaccinated status for influenza was independently associated with 34% lower odds of LLT use among American adults with ASCVD after adjustment for traditional factors linked to underuse of preventive therapies. This finding identifies a population with excess modifiable ASCVD risk, and supports investigation into non-traditional mechanisms driving underuse of preventive therapies, including fear-based misinformation.

## Abstract

Unvaccinated Status for Influenza Predicts Non-use of Lipid Lowering Therapy (LLT)

Adjusted for age, sex, race/ethnicity, BMI, income, education, language, state/territory, diabetes, hypertension, chronic kidney disease, ASCVD, smoking, alcohol use, health insurance, financial burden, personal relationship with a healthcare provider, and timing of most-recent preventive health visit. Analysis was weighted to account for survey design and to reflect national population estimates.

OR = odds ratio; CI = confidence interval; ASCVD = atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease

## Introduction

Atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) is the leading cause of death, morbidity, and healthcare utilization in the United States (US).1 Lipid lowering therapies (LLT)—primarily statins—are highly effective in preventing and treating ASCVD.2-5 Despite their established safety and affordability, many with patients with strong indications do not use LLT, including those with established ASCVD.6,7

Influenza immunization, besides reducing serious infections, also reduces major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE), cardiovascular mortality, and all-cause mortality in those with prior myocardial infarction (MI).8-12 The American Heart Association (AHA) and American College of Cardiology (ACC) have made influenza vaccination a class I recommendation for secondary prevention of ASCVD. Despite this, half of those with established ASCVD do not receive the annual influenza vaccine.10

It is not known whether being unvaccinated for influenza is associated with non-use of LLT. However, a particularly strong association may exist on the basis that both vaccines and statins are frequently the subject of fear-based misinformation and sensationalized accounts of adverse effects in both traditional mass media and social media platforms.13-23

We therefore evaluated whether influenza vaccination status was associated with LLT use among individuals with ASCVD in a large and nationally representative survey of American adults. We hypothesized that unvaccinated individuals would have lower use of LLT even after accounting for traditional factors associated with underuse of preventive therapies. Understanding this association has the potential to identify a population with excess modifiable ASCVD risk and to guide individual- and population-level efforts to support the use of high-value preventive therapies.

## Methods

### Data Source

The Behavioral Risk Factor Surveillance System (BRFSS) is a cross-sectional, annual survey conducted by the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.24 Data are collected by telephone interview from adults aged 18 years and older in all US states, the District of Columbia, Puerto Rico, Guam, and the US Virgin Islands. BRFSS employs a complex sampling design to obtain nationally representative estimates. Core modules of the survey cover a range of health-related behaviors, chronic conditions, and healthcare access. BRFSS datasets are publicly available and de-identified. The Institutional Review Board (IRB) of the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health determined that this study did not require IRB oversight.

We combined BRFSS data from 2017, 2019, and 2021. These years were selected because the core BRFSS questionnaire included sections on both immunizations and cholesterol. The response rates were 44.9%, 50.0%, and 44.6% in 2017, 2019, and 2021 respectively.24 Response rates were calculated as the proportion of all eligible and likely eligible people, in keeping with the American Association for Public Opinion Research (AAPOR) guidelines.25 Notably, Florida was excluded from the 2021 dataset due to a failure to meet the BRFSS data collection minimums.

### Analytic Sample

Our sample included all participants aged 40 to 75 years with a self-reported history of ASCVD, including coronary artery disease, angina pectoris, myocardial infarction, and stroke. Pregnant participants were excluded. Those with missing responses were excluded from the primary complete case analysis, but were included in the sensitivity analysis using multiple imputation for missing data.

### Exposures and covariates

Uptake of influenza vaccination was defined by an affirmative response to the question: “During the past 12 months, have you had either a flu vaccine that was sprayed in your nose or flu shot injected into your arm?” Use of LLT was defined by an affirmative response to the question: “Are you currently taking medicine prescribed by your doctor or other health professional for your cholesterol?” All responses other than “yes” or “no” were classified as missing.

Covariates included the following demographics and health conditions: age, sex, race/ethnicity, body mass index (BMI), income, education, language, state/territory, diabetes, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, smoking, and alcohol use. Age groups were categorized as follows: 40-49, 50-59, 60-69, and 70-75 years. BMI was categorized as underweight (<18 Kg/m2), normal weight (18-25 Kg/m2), overweight (26-30 Kg/m2), or obese (>30 Kg/m2). Race and ethnicity were categorized as “Hispanic”, “Black, Non-Hispanic”, “White, Non-Hispanic”, “Multiracial, Non-Hispanic”, or “Other, Non-Hispanic.” Income was categorized as less than $15K/year, $15-25K/year; $25-35K/year; $35-50K/year, or greater than $50K+/year. Education was categorized as less than high school, high school graduate, some college, or college graduate. Smoking was dichotomized as current smoking or not. Alcohol use was dichotomized as “heavy” (> 14 standard drinks/week for males or >7 drinks/week for females) or “not heavy”.

Healthcare access covariates included: health insurance status, financial burden, personal relationship with a healthcare provider, and timing of most-recent preventive healthcare visit. Insurance status was dichotomized as uninsured or any health insurance. High financial burden was dichotomized as “yes” or “no” to the question: “Was there a time in the past 12 months when you needed to see a doctor but could not because you could not afford it?” A personal relationship with a clinician was defined as having at least one person “you think of as a personal health care provider.” Timing of the last preventive healthcare visit was categorized as within the past 1 year, 2 years, 5 years, or more than 5 years/never.

Hypertension was determined by self-report, categorizing responses of “only while pregnant,” “borderline hypertension,” and “pre-hypertension” as not hypertensive. To capture blood pressure medication use patterns, we created a variable with 3 levels: not hypertensive, hypertensive taking medication, and hypertensive not taking medication.

### Statistical Analysis

We used survey weights in all estimations to account for selection probabilities, oversampling, and response rates. We compared covariates between influenza-vaccinated and unvaccinated participants using weighted percentages.

Of the 1,307,603 participants in the pooled BRFSS surveys, 97,829 individuals met the inclusion criteria. Data on LLT use were missing for 26,004 participants (26% weighted) and data on influenza vaccination were missing for 7,225 participants (8.6% weighted). Participants with missing data were excluded from the primary complete case analysis, but were included in our sensitivity analysis using multiple imputation for missing data.

We performed univariate logistic regression to evaluate the unadjusted association between influenza vaccine status and cholesterol medication use. We then used sequential multivariable logistic regression models to adjust for potential confounders chosen a priori based on their known or expected associations with vaccine uptake and cholesterol medication use.

Model 1 accounted for the following socio-demographic features and health conditions: age, sex, race/ethnicity, body mass index (BMI), income, education, language, state/territory, diabetes, hypertension, chronic kidney disease, hyperlipidemia, smoking, and alcohol use. Model 2 built upon Model 1 with the following additional healthcare access variables: health insurance status, financial burden, personal relationship with a healthcare provider, and timing of the most recent preventive healthcare visit. Model 2 also included a variable to account for the use of other cardiovascular therapies, specifically anti-hypertensive medication in those with self-reported hypertension.

We performed likelihood ratio tests on nested models to assess for effect modification by hyperlipidemia, age, sex, year, race, language, and state-level political leanings based on presidential election results from 2020.

As a sensitivity analysis, we performed multiple imputation to account for missing observations. We ran the univariate regression and sequential multivariable regression models on the imputed dataset to assess for bias to due non-random missingness.

All analyses were performed using R statistical software (version 4.2.2) within the R Studio environment version 2022.7.1.554.32 Analysis and presentation of complex survey data was facilitated with the survey and gtsummary packages.33,34

## Results

The characteristics of the study population are displayed in Table 1 with weighted percentages. Among the 66,923 BRFSS participants with ASCVD in our primary analysis, 55% reported receiving an influenza vaccine in the past year, and 76% reported taking LLT. Unvaccinated individuals were overall younger, had lower educational attainment, and had less access to healthcare. Among unvaccinated individuals, 70% reported LLT use compared with 81% of vaccinated individuals.

The unadjusted analysis and multivariable adjusted logistic regression models are shown in Table 2. In the unadjusted analysis, influenza unvaccinated status was associated with lower LLT use (OR 0.54; 95% CI 0.50, 0.58; p<0.001). In the multivariable regression model adjusting for basic demographics and co-morbidities (Model 1), this association attenuated slightly but remained statistically significant (OR 0.58; 95% CI 0.52, 0.64; p<0.001). In our second model (Model 2), which additionally adjusted for health care access and use of other cardiovascular medications the association remained robust with a 34% reduction in the odds of LLT usage (OR 0.66; 95% CI 0.60, 0.74; p<0.001).

The sensitivity analysis with multiple imputation provided similar results. Influenza unvaccinated status was associated with lower cholesterol medication use in the unadjusted analysis of the imputed dataset (OR 0.55, 95% CI 0.52, 0.59), adjusted according to Model 1 (OR 0.64, 95% CI 0.59, 0.70, p<0.001), and in the fully adjusted analysis of the imputed dataset according to Model 2 (OR 0.73; 95% CI 0.66, 0.79, p<0.001).

Figure 1 demonstrates our subgroup analysis under Model 2. There was no statistically significant effect modification by age, sex, year, race, language, state-level political leanings, or hyperlipidemia status.

## Discussion

In this large, cross-sectional, nationally representative sample of US adults aged 40 to 75 years with self-reported ASCVD between 2017 and 2021, we observed a robust association between influenza unvaccinated status and non-use of LLT. The association was similar across all subgroups.

To our knowledge, the present study is the first to demonstrate this association in a nationally representative sample of participants with established ASCVD. Prior smaller studies examining predictors of statin use have not included influenza vaccination status.7,26,27 While previous research on the “healthy user” phenomenon has shown that most preventive health behaviors, including primary prevention statins and vaccines, tend to associate with one another,36 our findings are distinct. Unlike prior work, the present study demonstrates an independent association between influenza vaccination and LLT use after adjustment for other multifaceted measures of preventive health engagement, including self-reported use of other cardiovascular medications to account for the “healthy user” phenomenon. Moreover, prior work has not focused on the high-risk population with ASCVD for which both LLT and influenza immunization have demonstrated a mortality benefit.

The present analysis does not provide an explanation for the independent association between influenza unvaccinated status and non-use of LLT, but it does provide grounds for hypothesis generation. It is possible that traditional risk factors for underuse of preventive therapies are incompletely captured in BRFSS surveys. However, BRFSS includes multiple validated instruments in these domains and the association remained robust after statistical adjustment for these domains, as well as adjustment for use of other cardiovascular medications.28,29 Therefore, it is likely that there are unmeasured, non-traditional factors driving use patterns of both the influenza vaccine and LLT.

These non-traditional factors might include patients’ exposure to forms of fear-based misinformation that uniquely target these therapies.14,23 Additional possibilities include a generalized distrust of medical institutions or susceptibility to the nocebo effect—the perception of adverse effects on the basis of expectations rather than pharmacology—which is known to affect both vaccines and LLT.15,30,31 Misinformation and sensationalized media accounts may also influence prescribers, resulting in affected clinicians being less likely to recommend vaccines and LLT.

Regardless of the reason, the strong association in use patterns between these two distinct yet similarly impactful means of secondary prevention has implications for both clinical practice and public health research. Unvaccinated individuals with ASCVD who are also non-users of LLT represent a population with excess cardiovascular risk that is highly modifiable. Further investigation into the reason for the association between influenza vaccination and LLT use may lead to elucidating non-traditional risk factors for underuse of preventive therapy.

While a range of interventions have demonstrated improvements in LLT use and influenza immunization rates, the benefits have generally been modest. Efforts to increase long-term use of CV medications have focused on patient-clinician communication, patient education, reminders/nudges, economic/logistical barriers, and frequent assessment of medication adherence.32-35 Efforts to increase vaccination have additionally included hospital- and community-level awareness interventions.36 One recent study targeting patients with ASCVD demonstrated that letters emphasizing the cardiovascular benefits of influenza vaccination resulted in improved immunization rates, but the improvements were small.37 Existing interventions may be limited in their effectiveness because they do not address the non-traditional risk factors detected by our study, highlighting the need to elucidate these factors as potential targets for future intervention.

### Strengths and Limitations

Strengths of this study are the large, nationally representative sample, and detailed survey data covering demographics, social determinants, access to care, and preventive health behaviors. Strengths also include the identification of a novel association between two of the most effective yet underused methods of reducing morbidity and mortality in individuals with underlying ASCVD. Several limitations also bear consideration. BRFSS does not include prescription data, medical recommendations, physiologic measurements, or laboratory values; therefore, we relied on self-report, which is susceptible to recall bias. However, self-report also has advantages over other measures of medication use, such as prescription fill records, which can be incomplete and miss instances where a patients fills a prescription but does not take the medication. Importantly, self-report may capture instances when a patient declines a prescription for LLT, which is common and not captured by most other methods.38 Response bias inherent in BRFSS may have selected for respondents who were more trusting of medical institutions and therefore willing to complete a survey administered by the CDC, which is consistent with the overall rates of reported LLT being higher than in most other studies.6,39 However, we believe that a sample enriched for more trusting individuals would, if anything, attenuate the association of interest.

Our analysis was limited by missing data on LLT use, however, our results were robust to a sensitivity analysis using multiple imputation to account for missing data. Moreover, the rate of missing data on cholesterol medication use was extremely low among participants who reported hyperlipidemia (0.5%) and our findings were unchanged in the subgroup with hyperlipidemia. Finally, as with all observational studies, the ability to demonstrate causation is limited due to residual and unmeasured confounding. Yet, this study was not aimed at proving causation since a direct causal link is implausible. In fact, the value of our study is that it demonstrates the existence of important unmeasured factors associated with both vaccination status and LLT use and generates hypotheses as to what they might be.

## Conclusion

Unvaccinated status for influenza was associated with 34% lower odds of LLT use among American adults with ASCVD. This association was not fully explained by traditional risk factors for underuse of preventive therapies. Unvaccinated adults with ASCVD who are non-users of LLT represent a group with excess modifiable cardiovascular risk. Our findings support further investigation into non-traditional factors affecting use of preventive therapies, such as growing trends in fear-based misinformation.
